questions.stem: International law is best described as:
options: the rules set by transnational corporations for trade between their branches
the treaties and customary rules that govern relations between states
the laws of the most powerful state, which all other states must follow
the domestic laws that each state passes about its own citizens' travel
questions.explanation: International law is made up mainly of treaties that states agree to and of customary rules that states accept as binding. It is not imposed by one powerful state, and it binds states rather than being set by corporations.

questions.stem: The rules-based international order refers to:
options: an alliance of democratic states that enforces their values on all other states
a ranking of states according to the size of their economies and armed forces
a shared commitment by states to conduct their relations according to agreed rules
a single world government with a parliament that makes laws binding on every person on Earth
questions.explanation: The rules-based order is the framework of international law, treaties and institutions, such as the UN, through which states agree to manage their relations and settle disputes. There is no world government standing above states.

questions.stem: Global governance is best described as:
options: a world government with a parliament elected by the citizens of every one of its member states
the control that the largest state exercises over the decisions of smaller states
the domestic system of government used in most of the world's liberal democracies
the institutions, rules and processes through which actors cooperate on global issues
questions.explanation: Global governance is the network of institutions, such as the UN, IMF and WTO, together with international law and processes, that lets states and other actors cooperate on issues no state can manage alone. It is not a world government.

questions.stem: Which principle of democracy is most directly expressed when voters can remove a government at a regular election?
options: Economic liberalism and free markets
Separation of church and state
Accountability of governments to the people
Respect for the sovereignty of other states
questions.explanation: Regular elections in which a government can lose office make it answerable to the people for its decisions. Respect for other states' sovereignty concerns relations between states, not the relationship between a government and its voters.

questions.stem: Economic liberalism is best described as a commitment to:
options: free markets, private property and limited state control of the economy
state ownership of all major industries and central planning of production
protecting individual rights and freedoms and limiting government power
giving each citizen an equal share of the nation's income and wealth
questions.explanation: Economic liberalism favours free markets, private property and free trade, with limited government intervention. Protecting individual rights and limiting government power is political liberalism, a related but distinct idea.

questions.stem: Political liberalism is best described as a commitment to:
options: protecting individual rights and freedoms and placing limits on government power
allowing markets to set prices and wages with as little government regulation as possible
uniting all citizens behind one official ideology chosen by the ruling party
basing the laws of the state on the teachings of its majority religion
questions.explanation: Political liberalism centres on individual rights, such as freedom of speech and association, and on constitutional limits on government. Letting markets set prices with little regulation is economic liberalism.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a check on governmental power?
options: A government extends its own term in office by passing a new law
A leader appoints loyal party members to run the electoral commission
A ruling party introduces laws that require journalists to hold a licence
An independent court rules that a government decision was unlawful
questions.explanation: Independent courts that can rule against the government limit its power and hold it to the law. A government extending its own term or controlling the electoral body removes checks rather than creating them.

questions.stem: A government refuses to release the reasons for a major decision, saying national security requires secrecy, though no security issue is involved. Which democratic principle is most directly at risk?
options: Economic liberalism
Free, fair and multiparty elections
Transparency of decision-making
Respect for the sovereignty of states
questions.explanation: Transparency requires that the public can see how and why decisions are made, so they can judge them. Elections may still be free and fair while a government conceals its reasoning, so that principle is not the one most directly at risk.

questions.stem: Respect for state sovereignty can come into conflict with the protection of human rights because:
options: sovereign states are banned by international law from signing any treaty on human rights
human rights can be protected only by states that have given up their sovereignty to the UN
respecting sovereignty requires every state to adopt the same system of government
protecting people from abuse may require outside actors to intervene in a state's internal affairs
questions.explanation: Sovereignty implies non-interference in a state's internal affairs, but stopping serious human rights abuses may require other states or institutions to step in. Sovereign states can and do sign human rights treaties; they agree to limits on themselves by doing so.

questions.stem: An authoritarian system is one in which:
options: power is shared among many parties that compete in regular free and fair elections for office
power is held by the people, who vote directly on every law instead of electing a parliament
power is divided between national and regional governments under a written constitution
power is concentrated in a leader or small group that the people cannot remove through free elections
questions.explanation: Authoritarian rulers concentrate power and are not accountable to the people through genuine elections, and they limit opposition and dissent. Dividing power between national and regional governments is federalism, which can exist in democracies or not.

questions.stem: A totalitarian regime differs from other authoritarian regimes mainly because it:
options: allows independent courts to strike down its laws when they breach citizens' rights
relies only on economic performance and never on coercion to keep itself in power
seeks control over almost every part of public and private life through an official ideology
holds regular multiparty elections in which the ruling party can lose office to one of its rivals
questions.explanation: All authoritarian regimes limit political freedom, but totalitarian regimes go further, using an official ideology, mass mobilisation, propaganda and surveillance to control society, the economy and private life. Neither kind of regime allows genuine electoral competition.

questions.stem: Populism is best described as an ideology or style of politics that:
options: holds that all people share one global community with duties across borders
bases the laws and leadership of the state on religious teachings
presents politics as a struggle between 'the people' and a corrupt elite
seeks to place all major industries under state ownership and planning
questions.explanation: Populists claim to speak for the ordinary, 'pure' people against an elite they portray as corrupt or out of touch. Populism can be found on the left or the right, because it is about this framing rather than any particular economic program.

questions.stem: Populism can become a challenge to liberal democracy when populist leaders:
options: allow a free press to criticise them and answer journalists' questions at public events
hand over power peacefully to their rivals after losing an election to another party
claim to be the only true voice of the people and attack courts and the media as enemies
accept rulings against them by independent courts and respond through the proper appeal process
questions.explanation: By claiming that only they represent the people, populist leaders can treat opponents, judges and journalists as illegitimate and weaken the checks that limit power. Accepting court rulings, a free press and peaceful transfers of power are signs of respect for democratic norms.

questions.stem: In a system of governance informed by theism, such as a theocracy:
options: the state is required by its constitution to keep religion entirely out of public life
the ruling party bans all religion and replaces it with a secular official ideology
every citizen votes directly on the laws that the clergy propose to the parliament
religious authority or religious law is a central source of political legitimacy
questions.explanation: Theism as a basis for governance draws the authority to rule, and often the law itself, from religious belief and religious leaders. Keeping religion out of public life is the separation of church and state, the opposite approach.

questions.stem: A cosmopolitan view of global governance would most likely support:
options: each state acting only in its own national interest in global forums
closing borders to protect a nation's culture from outside influences
stronger international institutions to protect human rights in every state
strict non-interference in other states' internal affairs in all circumstances
questions.explanation: Cosmopolitans believe all people share one moral community, so they favour global institutions and rules that protect rights everywhere. Acting only in the national interest is the realist view that cosmopolitans reject.

questions.stem: An illiberal democracy is a system in which:
options: elections are held, but civil liberties, media freedom and checks on power are weakened
there are no elections, and a military council governs the state by issuing decrees
elections are free and fair, and courts strongly protect the rights of minorities
the people vote directly on every law, so no parliament or courts are needed
questions.explanation: Illiberal democracies keep elections but erode the liberal features of democracy, such as independent courts, a free press and protected rights. A state with no elections ruled by a military council is authoritarian.

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly distinguishes a liberal democracy from an authoritarian system?
options: A head of state who represents the nation at international meetings
Genuine competition for power through free, fair, multiparty elections
A written constitution that names the state's institutions and their roles
A national parliament that meets regularly in the capital to pass laws
questions.explanation: Many authoritarian states have written constitutions, parliaments and heads of state, so those features do not distinguish them. What they lack is genuine competition in which the people can remove the government at free and fair elections.

questions.stem: State Q holds regular elections with several parties. However, the ruling party controls most media, its leader appoints all judges, and critics are often harassed. State Q is best described as:
options: a liberal democracy, because it holds regular elections in which several parties compete
a totalitarian state, because it seeks to control every aspect of its citizens' private lives
a theocracy, because its leader draws legitimacy from religious authority and religious law
an illiberal democracy, because elections are held but liberal protections are eroded
questions.explanation: State Q keeps the outward form of multiparty elections, but control of the media, a judiciary dependent on the leader and harassment of critics show that liberal checks and freedoms are being eroded. Holding elections alone does not make a state a liberal democracy.

questions.stem: State R has no national elections and is ruled by a military council that issues decrees, but citizens may practise their religion and run businesses freely. State R is best described as:
options: an illiberal democracy, because it holds elections but limits some civil liberties
a liberal democracy, because its citizens enjoy religious and economic freedoms
authoritarian, because power is concentrated and not accountable through elections
totalitarian, because the state seeks control of every aspect of its citizens' lives
questions.explanation: The council holds power without elections, which makes State R authoritarian. It is not totalitarian, because it leaves religion and business largely alone rather than trying to control all of society, and it cannot be any kind of democracy without elections.

questions.stem: In many authoritarian systems, power is concentrated rather than separated. This means that:
options: the courts may strike down any law that the executive proposes
the legislature can remove the leader at any time by a simple vote
regional governments hold most power and the centre holds little
the executive controls or overrides the legislature and the courts
questions.explanation: Concentration of power means the executive dominates, so the legislature and courts cannot act as independent checks on it. Courts striking down laws and a legislature able to remove the leader are features of separated, checked power.

questions.stem: Which feature is typical of liberal democracies but often absent in theocratic systems?
options: A head of state who leads the country's government
A set of laws that applies to the whole of the state
Government ministries responsible for areas of policy
The separation of religious institutions from the state
questions.explanation: Liberal democracies generally keep the state separate from religious institutions, so that political authority does not depend on religious belief. All states, including theocracies, have laws and government ministries.

questions.stem: The United Nations was founded in 1945 mainly to:
options: replace the governments of all its member states with a single elected global government
set the exchange rates of all national currencies against the US dollar
try individuals accused of war crimes committed during the Second World War
maintain international peace and security and promote cooperation between states
questions.explanation: The UN Charter sets out the UN's main purposes as maintaining international peace and security, developing friendly relations between states and promoting cooperation, including on human rights. The UN does not govern its member states.

questions.stem: Resolutions of the United Nations General Assembly are generally:
options: valid only if every member state votes in favour of the resolution
recommendations that are not legally binding on member states
binding on all member states and enforced by the International Court of Justice
binding only on the five permanent members of the Security Council
questions.explanation: In the General Assembly each member state has one vote, and its resolutions carry moral and political weight but are generally not binding. Binding decisions on peace and security are made by the Security Council.

questions.stem: Critics argue that the UN Security Council can weaken the rules-based order because:
options: non-permanent members can veto any resolution that the five permanent members have agreed upon
the Council has no power to authorise sanctions or the use of force against any member state
its resolutions must be approved by a majority of the General Assembly before they take effect
a permanent member can veto action even when it or an ally is accused of breaching international law
questions.explanation: The veto lets each of the five permanent members block action against itself or its allies, so the Council may be unable to respond when a powerful state breaks the rules. Only permanent members have a veto, and the Council can authorise sanctions and force.

questions.stem: The International Court of Justice:
options: lends money to member states that face a financial crisis
settles legal disputes between states and gives advisory opinions
tries individuals accused of genocide and crimes against humanity
hears appeals from the highest courts of each UN member state
questions.explanation: The ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the UN; it decides disputes between states and gives advisory opinions on legal questions referred by UN bodies. Trying individuals for genocide and crimes against humanity is the role of the International Criminal Court.

questions.stem: Why can the International Court of Justice struggle to uphold international law?
options: It may hear only cases about trade between members of the World Trade Organization
Its rulings must be approved by the General Assembly before they have any legal effect
It can decide a dispute only where the states involved have accepted its jurisdiction
All of its judges are chosen by the state that brings each case, so its rulings are not trusted
questions.explanation: The ICJ's jurisdiction depends on state consent, so a state that has not accepted it cannot be brought before the Court, and the Court has no means of its own to enforce its judgments. Its judges are elected by the UN General Assembly and Security Council, not chosen by the parties.

questions.stem: The International Criminal Court prosecutes:
options: corporations accused of polluting rivers and oceans across national borders
national governments that fail to repay the loans made to them by the International Monetary Fund
individuals accused of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression
states that breach the trade agreements they have signed with other states
questions.explanation: Set up under the Rome Statute, the ICC tries individuals, including leaders, for the most serious international crimes. Disputes between states are heard by the International Court of Justice or, for trade, through the WTO.

questions.stem: Under the principle of complementarity, the International Criminal Court:
options: takes over every case of a serious crime from national courts as soon as it is reported
hears appeals from national criminal courts in the states that have joined the court
shares each case with the International Court of Justice and gives a joint verdict
acts only when national courts are unwilling or unable to genuinely prosecute a case
questions.explanation: Complementarity means national courts have the first responsibility to prosecute international crimes, and the ICC steps in only when a state is unwilling or unable to do so genuinely. The ICC is not an appeal court above national courts.

questions.stem: Which is a significant limitation on the power of the International Criminal Court?
options: Its jurisdiction covers only crimes committed in Europe by the citizens of European states
Each of its decisions must be approved by the permanent members of the Security Council
It depends on states to arrest and hand over suspects, because it has no police force of its own
It can try only former heads of state, and only after they have left office in their home state
questions.explanation: The ICC cannot make arrests itself, so suspects in states that will not cooperate can avoid trial. Its jurisdiction is not limited to Europe or to former leaders, and its judgments do not need Security Council approval.

questions.stem: The International Monetary Fund mainly supports the global economy by:
options: printing a global currency that replaces member states' own currencies
lending to states in financial crisis, often on conditions about economic policy
setting the exact tariffs that each member state may charge on the goods it imports
funding the peacekeeping operations authorised by the Security Council
questions.explanation: The IMF lends to member states facing balance-of-payments or financial crises and usually attaches conditions, such as budget or economic reforms. Trade rules on tariffs are the business of the World Trade Organization.

questions.stem: Critics argue that decision-making in the International Monetary Fund is undemocratic because:
options: decisions are made by the UN General Assembly rather than by the IMF's own members
its loans are decided by a ballot of the citizens of the member states receiving them
voting power is weighted by each member's financial quota, which favours wealthy states
each member state has one equal vote, so very small states can outvote large economies
questions.explanation: Each member's votes in the IMF depend mainly on its quota, which reflects the size of its economy, so wealthy states hold most of the voting power. Critics say this gives developing states, which are most often the borrowers, too little say.

questions.stem: The World Trade Organization reinforces the rules-based order mainly by:
options: deciding which states may become members of the United Nations General Assembly
setting rules for trade and providing a process to settle trade disputes between members
lending money to member states whose currencies have collapsed during a financial crisis
prosecuting business leaders who break the trade laws of their own home countries
questions.explanation: The WTO administers agreed trade rules and gives members a process to resolve trade disputes through rules rather than retaliation. Emergency lending to states in financial crisis is the role of the IMF.

questions.stem: The difference between misinformation and disinformation is that disinformation is:
options: false information spread deliberately in order to deceive
false information spread by mistake, without meaning to deceive
accurate information that is reported without any context
information that is false but too minor to cause any harm
questions.explanation: Disinformation is false information spread on purpose to mislead, for example by a state seeking to disrupt another's election. Misinformation is false information spread without intent to deceive, often by people who believe it.

questions.stem: Hackers working for a foreign state break into an electoral commission's computer systems and leak voters' details. This is an example of:
options: cyber interference
populism
economic liberalism
complementarity
questions.explanation: Cyber interference is the use of digital means, such as hacking or online influence campaigns, to disrupt or manipulate another state's political processes. Populism is a style of politics, not a technique of interference.

questions.stem: Before an election, thousands of fake social media accounts run from overseas spread false claims that votes will not be counted fairly. The most likely consequence for democracy is:
options: the automatic cancellation of the election by an international court
reduced public trust in the election and in the legitimacy of its result
an increase in voters' confidence in the independence of the electoral body
a transfer of the state's sovereignty to the state running the fake accounts
questions.explanation: Disinformation aimed at the voting process seeks to make citizens doubt the result, which weakens the legitimacy of whoever wins and may reduce participation. A foreign state spreading false claims does not gain sovereignty over the target state.

questions.stem: Some governments argue that democracy and human rights reflect Western values rather than universal ones. This challenge to the spread of democracy is described as:
options: complementarity
perceived western cultural bias
cosmopolitanism
economic liberalism
questions.explanation: The claim that democratic principles are a Western cultural product, unsuited to other societies, is the challenge of perceived western cultural bias. Cosmopolitanism holds the opposite, that rights belong to all people as members of one human community.

questions.stem: Which response best counters the argument that human rights are a purely Western idea?
options: Human rights apply only in states that already have a liberal democratic system of government
Only Western states took part in writing international law, so its rules reflect their values
Democracy suits only wealthy states, so it cannot be expected to spread beyond the West
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by states from many regions and cultures
questions.explanation: The Universal Declaration was drafted with contributions from people of many backgrounds and adopted in 1948 by UN members from several continents, which supports the claim that its rights are universal. Saying only Western states wrote international law would support the bias argument rather than counter it.

questions.stem: Authoritarian governments often justify limits on democracy by claiming that:
options: a free press is essential for holding their own ministers to account
strong central control is needed for stability, security or economic growth
free and fair elections are needed to give their rule the consent of the governed
independent courts should be able to overturn any decision they make
questions.explanation: A common legitimising narrative of authoritarian rulers is that order and prosperity require a firm hand, and that open competition would bring chaos. Endorsing free elections, independent courts and a free press would undercut their own concentration of power.

questions.stem: Which is most likely to be a cause of rising support for populism within a democracy?
options: A strong, independent media that is trusted by most of the population
Low economic inequality and secure employment for most of the workforce
A widespread belief that elites ignore ordinary people's economic concerns
High public trust in the parliament, the courts and the public service
questions.explanation: Populism draws on resentment of elites, so a sense that those in power ignore ordinary people, often linked to inequality or economic insecurity, feeds it. High trust in institutions and widely shared prosperity tend to reduce its appeal.

questions.stem: Which is most likely to be a consequence of democratic backsliding in a state?
options: Stronger protection of minority rights by the courts and parliament
Greater transparency in how the government makes its decisions
More competitive elections in which the ruling party may lose
Weaker checks on executive power, such as courts and a free press
questions.explanation: Democratic backsliding is the gradual erosion of democratic institutions, often by elected leaders who weaken courts, the media and electoral integrity. Stronger rights protection, greater transparency and more competitive elections are the opposite of backsliding.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a problem with the current rules-based international order?
options: The UN Charter commits its members to settle their disputes with each other by peaceful means
The International Court of Justice gives advisory opinions when asked by UN bodies
States can bring trade disputes to the World Trade Organization for settlement
Powerful states sometimes break international law without facing effective consequences
questions.explanation: The order depends on states obeying rules that no central authority can fully enforce, so powerful states may ignore them with little cost, which undermines confidence in the system. A commitment to peaceful settlement and access to dispute settlement are normal features of the order.
